T1: Performance‑oriented motorcycle enthusiasts will purchase high‑performance Brembo brakes directly, justifying a differentiated consumer proposition. Who benefits: Enthusiast riders seeking superior braking performance and a premium brand experience.. Why behaviour changes: These riders value motorsport heritage, adjustability, and the status associated with top‑tier components; they are willing to pay a premium for proven performance.. How value is captured: Brembo can capture value through premium pricing, direct‑to‑consumer sales channels (e.g., e‑commerce, specialty retailers), and brand extension into lifestyle accessories.. Assumptions: There is a measurable segment of motorcycle owners willing to spend €750 for high‑performance brakes.; These enthusiasts are willing to buy directly from Brembo rather than through dealers.; The market is large enough to justify dedicated consumer marketing and distribution.. Predictions: A survey of 500 motorcycle enthusiasts would show at least 30% indicating intent to purchase a €750 Brembo brake kit within 12 months.; Sales of a direct‑to‑consumer offering would generate at least €5 million in revenue in the first year, assuming 1,000 units sold..

T2: Urban and everyday consumers will purchase Brembo brakes for e‑bikes and SSVs because they value safety, reliability, and a premium brand associated with performance, justifying a differentiated consumer proposition. Who benefits: Urban commuters, e‑bike owners, and SSV riders seeking reliable braking solutions that signal quality and safety.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers prioritize safety and performance in daily transportation; they are willing to pay a premium for trusted, tested components that reduce risk and enhance ride confidence.. How value is captured: Brembo can capture value through premium pricing, partnerships with e‑bike manufacturers, and direct‑to‑consumer sales channels (e.g., online, specialty retailers) for these specific use cases.. Assumptions: There is a measurable segment of urban commuters and SSV owners willing to spend €300‑€500 for reliable brakes.; These consumers are willing to buy directly from Brembo rather than through dealers for these specific applications.; The market is large enough to justify dedicated consumer marketing and distribution for e‑bikes and SSVs.. Predictions: A survey of 500 urban commuters and SSV owners would show at least 25% indicating intent to purchase a Brembo brake kit for their vehicle within 12 months.; Sales of a direct‑to‑consumer offering for e‑bikes and SSVs would generate at least €3 million in revenue in the first year, assuming 2,000 units sold..

Test "Consumer Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Lapp Home Automation" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners in Germany who own electric vehicles and have home charging installations. They are randomly assigned to one of two scenarios: (A) a premium, integrated Lapp-branded home‑automation charging kit (e.g., a cable and connector set marketed as a single, co‑branded product) priced at €250; (B) a generic Lapp cable and connector set (same technical specifications) priced at €150. Both scenarios include a brief product description emphasizing Lapp’s. Sample: 200 participants (100 per scenario) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and EV ownership status.. Measure: Primary outcome: willingness to pay (WTP) difference between the premium integrated kit and the generic kit (WTP premium). Secondary outcomes: purchase intent (binary) and perceived reliability (1‑10 scale).. Predictions: T1: WTP premium ≥ €100 (i.e., participants value the integrated premium kit at least €100 more than the generic kit).; T2: WTP premium ≤ €50 (i.e., participants do not value the integrated premium kit more than the generic kit).. Decision rule: If WTP premium ≥ €100, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting premium, integrated home‑automation charging. If WTP premium ≤ €50, maintain the current B2B focus. If WTP premium is between €50 and €100, conduct a smaller pilot to validate before committing resources.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct a low‑cost pilot test (e.g., the proposed willingness‑to‑pay survey) to validate demand before committing resources. If the pilot shows a willingness‑to‑pay premium of at least €100, proceed to develop a premium, integrated home‑automation charging kit; otherwise, maintain the B2B focus. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated result SYN-D concerns warehouse packing errors and does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or integration of Lapp components in home automation. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct a low‑cost pilot test (e.g., the proposed willingness‑to‑pay survey) to validate demand before committing resources. If the pilot shows a willingness‑to‑pay premium of at least €100, proceed to develop a premium, integrated home‑automation charging kit; otherwise, maintain the B2B focus. Target customer: Private electric car drivers and homeowners seeking integrated charging solutions and smart‑home connectivity.. Value proposition: Premium, reliable, integrated Lapp‑branded home‑automation charging components that simplify installation and reduce compatibility issues, sold through existing consumer channels or bundled with consumer brands.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed willingness‑to‑pay survey with 200 participants (100 per scenario) to measure premium willingness to pay and purchase intent.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market, willingness to pay a premium for integrated components, and the ability to reach homeowners through existing distribution channels are uncertain.. Would change if: If the survey shows a willingness‑to‑pay premium of at least €100, indicating consumer demand for integrated premium kits.; If a partner consumer brand approaches Lapp to co‑develop a bundled offering, signaling market pull from established consumer channels.; If new evidence shows that Lapp already sells consumer‑grade components through its own e‑commerce or retail partners, reducing the need for a new entry.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 72 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific consumer use case (e.g., home storage, small‑business inventory management).; 2) Expand the existing B2B portfolio into adjacent industrial segments (e.g., food‑processing, e‑commerce fulfillment) without a consumer focus.; 3) No expansion – maintain current product and market focus, monitor consumer trends without investment.; 4) License Kardex’s technology to consumer brands or white‑label solutions for consumer markets..

T1: Consumers will adopt Kardex’s automated storage systems for home use if the price is comparable to existing consumer storage solutions (e.g., shelving, bins) and if the system offers clear productivity benefits (e.g., reduced time spent locating items). Who benefits: Homeowners and small businesses seeking efficient storage and retrieval of household goods.. Why behaviour changes: If the price is similar to alternative solutions and the benefits (time savings, reduced clutter) are demonstrated, consumers will switch from traditional storage to automated systems.. How value is captured: Kardex would sell direct‑to‑consumer kits or subscription‑based services, capturing value through hardware sales, installation fees, and recurring maintenance.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for time‑saving storage solutions.; Installation and support costs can be priced attractively enough to offset higher hardware cost.; Kardex can reach individual buyers through online channels or retail partnerships.. Predictions: A survey of 500 households would show that at least 30% would consider purchasing a Kardex home storage kit if priced at €500–€800.; A pilot offering the kit at a discount would generate at least 200 pre‑orders within 4 weeks..

T2: Consumers will adopt Kardex’s automated storage systems for home use if they perceive the system as a status symbol or lifestyle enhancement, and are willing to pay a premium for design, convenience, and the ability to showcase personal organization. Who benefits: Affluent homeowners and early adopters who value aesthetics, convenience, and social signaling through home organization.. Why behaviour changes: If the system is marketed as a design element and lifestyle upgrade, consumers will choose it over conventional storage to signal status and personal taste, even at higher prices.. How value is captured: Kardex would sell premium, design‑focused kits through specialty retailers, online luxury platforms, and direct‑to‑consumer channels, capturing value through higher hardware margins and optional design‑service add‑ons.. Assumptions: Affluent consumers prioritize home aesthetics and convenience over cost.; Marketing can effectively frame the system as a lifestyle product.; Kardex can design and manufacture aesthetically differentiated kits without compromising core functionality.. Predictions: A survey of 500 affluent households would show that at least 20% would consider purchasing a Kardex home storage kit priced at €1,200–€1,500.; A limited‑edition designer kit would generate at least 100 pre‑orders within 4 weeks at that price point..

T1 neutral, from kardex-dealership-parts (company_assertion): "Kardex automated storage systems bring speed, structure, and visibility to dealership parts departments. They condense storage footprints, increase on-hand inventory, and allow service operations to run more efficiently—resulting in faster repairs, higher throughput, and increased customer satisfaction.". Does not show: The source demonstrates B2B value but does not address consumer willingness to pay for home storage or productivity benefits for households..

T2 neutral, from kardex-analogy-bumblebee (company_assertion): "Dishotsky said the point at which it becomes interesting is when the cost of Bumblebee's product comes down to equal what a company like Starcity would have otherwise paid to furnish a unit.". Does not show: The source discusses a real‑estate furniture storage product and its cost comparison, not consumer motivations for purchasing automated home storage as a status symbol or lifestyle enhancement..

Test "Home Storage Kit Pilot" between T1; T2. Method: Online pre‑order pilot with two price points and two marketing frames.. Sample: 500 Swiss households recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and region.. Measure: Number of pre‑orders placed at each price point and self‑reported primary motivation (productivity vs status/lifestyle).. Predictions: T1: At least 30% of participants will pre‑order the €500–€800 kit (productivity‑focused), and the remaining 70% will pre‑order the €1,200–€1,500 kit (status/lifestyle).; T2: At least 20% of participants will pre‑order the €1,200–€1,500 kit (status/lifestyle), and the remaining 80% will pre‑order the €500–€800 kit (productivity‑focused).. Decision rule: If the €1,200–€1,500 kit achieves at least 20% pre‑orders and the €500–€800 kit achieves at least 30% pre‑orders, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting status/lifestyle (supports T2). If the opposite pattern holds, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting productivity (supports T1). If neither threshold is met, recommend no expansion (. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed Home Storage Kit pilot to test consumer demand at two price points and two marketing frames. If the €500–€800 kit meets its 30% pre‑order threshold and the €1,200–€1,500 kit does not, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting productivity benefits. If the opposite pattern emerges, proceed to develop a status/lifestyle proposition. If neither threshold is met, recommend no Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing errors and does not address consumer demand, price sensitivity, or motivation for automated home storage. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: Consumers will adopt Kardex’s automated storage systems for home use if the price is comparable to existing consumer storage solutions (e.g., shelving, bins) and if the system offers clear productivity benefits (e.g., reduced time spent locating items).. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Run the proposed Home Storage Kit pilot to test consumer demand at two price points and two marketing frames. If the €500‑€800 kit meets its 30% pre‑order threshold and the €1,200‑€1,500 kit does not, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting productivity benefits. If the opposite pattern emerges, proceed to develop a status/lifestyle proposition. If neither threshold is met, recommend no Target customer: Swiss households seeking efficient home storage solutions, particularly those willing to pay a premium for time‑saving benefits.. Value proposition: A Kardex‑branded automated home storage kit that reduces clutter, saves time, and can be installed by local certified partners, sold at a price comparable to conventional storage alternatives but offering clear productivity gains.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the 12‑week pilot with 500 Swiss households, offering two price points and two marketing frames to measure pre‑order conversion and motivation.. Uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay a premium for automated home storage; the exact price point that triggers purchase; the competitive landscape of existing consumer storage solutions.. Would change if: If the pilot shows the €1,200‑€1,500 kit achieving at least 20% pre‑orders and the €500‑€800 kit fewer than 30%, shift focus to a status/lifestyle proposition.; If neither kit meets its threshold, abandon consumer expansion and maintain B2B focus.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand at a lower price point, adjust the value proposition and pricing accordingly.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Private electric car drivers will adopt Lapp’s charging solutions if the price is competitive and the installation is easy, because they value convenience and affordability. Who benefits: Private EV owners and Lapp Mobility GmbH through higher sales volume and margin.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers switch from expensive or complex charging options to straightforward, lower‑cost solutions when the total cost of ownership is reduced.. How value is captured: Lapp can increase unit sales by bundling accessories with cables, offering subscription or service contracts, and leveraging its existing global logistics network to reach consumers directly.. Assumptions: Price sensitivity is high among price‑sensitive EV buyers.; Installation ease is a critical purchase criterion for private users.; Lapp can meet the demand without significant new investment.. Predictions: A test offering a bundled cable‑charger kit at a price 10% below competitors will generate at least 20% more purchase intent among private EV owners.; Purchase intent will be lower if installation complexity is added as a requirement..

T2: Private electric car owners will adopt Lapp’s charging solutions if they receive incentives or subsidies from governments or utility providers, because these reduce the effective price and remove upfront purchase barriers. Who benefits: Private EV owners through lower cost of ownership, Lapp through increased volume sales and potential recurring revenue from service contracts.. Assumptions: Governments or utilities offer sufficient incentives to offset the base price.; Incentives are accessible and easily redeemed by private buyers.; Lapp can scale its consumer distribution without major new investment.. Test "Price vs Incentive Test for Private EV Charging" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice experiment with randomized exposure to price discount or government rebate incentive. Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1:Very unlikely, 7:Very likely).. Sample: 500 private electric car owners recruited via automotive forums and EV owner communities in Germany, balanced by age, gender, vehicle model, and geographic region.. Measure: Purchase intent (7-point scale) for a bundled cable‑charger kit priced at €250 without discount (base), and two variant versions: (1) 10% price discount (€225), (2) 20% government rebate (effectively €200 after tax rebate).. Predictions: T1: Price discount will generate at least 15 percentage points higher purchase intent than the base price, and the incentive will not significantly affect intent (difference <5 points).; T2: Incentive will generate at least 15 percentage points higher purchase intent than the base price, and the price discount will not significantly affect intent (difference <5 points).. Decision rule: If the price discount version achieves ≥30% higher intent than the base version, proceed with differentiated consumer proposition focused on price affordability. If the incentive version achieves ≥30% higher intent than the base version, proceed with. Cost: 12000 euros, 10 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 72 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Homebrewers and small-batch food producers will adopt Krones equipment primarily because they seek professional-grade performance and reliability that reduces waste and improves product consistency, leading to higher willingness to pay for premium equipment. Who benefits: Homebrewers and small-batch food producers seeking consistent, high‑quality output.. Why behaviour changes: These users currently use amateur or generic equipment and experience high variability in product quality and yield. They will switch to Krones when they recognize that professional‑grade machines reduce waste, improve efficiency, and can. How value is captured: Krones would capture value by selling higher‑margin machines directly to consumers or through specialty retailers, leveraging its reputation for quality and support.. Assumptions: Homebrewers and small‑batch producers have sufficient discretionary budget to purchase premium equipment.; They value consistency and quality over cost.; They trust brand reputation for reliability.. Predictions: Surveyed homebrewers will indicate willingness to pay a premium (e.g., 20% above generic equipment) for Krones machines.; Purchase intent will be higher for machines marketed as professional‑grade or "craft‑brewer approved.".

T2: Homebrewers and small-batch food producers will adopt Krones equipment primarily because they seek a premium, differentiated brand that signals quality and craftsmanship, leading to willingness to pay for design, aesthetics, and brand prestige. Who benefits: Homebrewers and small-batch food producers who value brand image and status.. Why behaviour changes: These users currently use generic or unbranded equipment and view product quality as functional; they will switch to Krones when they perceive the brand as a status symbol that distinguishes their output and attracts customers.. How value is captured: Krones would capture value by pricing machines at a premium, selling through specialty retailers or direct-to-consumer channels, and leveraging brand equity to justify higher margins.. Assumptions: Status and brand perception are important purchase drivers for this segment.; Consumers are willing to pay more for a brand that signals craftsmanship.; Krones can differentiate its equipment through design, finish, or marketing messaging.. Predictions: Surveyed homebrewers will rank brand prestige as a top purchase criterion.; Willingness to pay a premium (e.g., 15% above generic equipment) will be higher for branded Krones machines..

Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Homebrewers" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are recruited from a panel of U.S. homebrewers (n = 300). They are shown two Krones equipment options: a generic home-brew machine priced at $1,500 and a Krones professional-grade machine priced at $2,500 (or $2,200 with a premium finish). They are asked: "Which option would you purchase for your homebrewing setup?" and "What is the maximum price you would pay for a Krones machine?" The survey also collects demographic data (age, experience, income).. Sample: 300 U.S. homebrewers recruited via a panel provider, balanced for experience level.. Measure: Purchase choice (generic vs Krones) and maximum price willing to pay for Krones (in euros).. Predictions: T1: At least 60% of participants will choose the Krones professional-grade machine, and the average maximum price willing to pay will be at least 20% above the generic price (e.g., €1,800).; T2: At least 60% of participants will choose the Krones professional-grade machine, and the average maximum price willing to pay will be at least 15% above the generic price (e.g., €1,700).. Decision rule: If the proportion choosing Krones ≥ 60% and the average maximum price ≥ 1.20 × generic price, then evidence supports T1. If the proportion choosing Krones ≥ 60% and the average maximum price ≥ 1.15 × generic price, then evidence supports T2. If neither condition is met, evidence is insufficient to. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. First, conduct the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (Test X1) to validate whether homebrewers are willing to pay a premium for professional-grade equipment. If the survey confirms willingness (e.g., ≥60% choose Krones premium and average price ≥1.20x generic), proceed to develop a consumer proposition targeting homebrewers. If not, maintain the current B2B Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated test (SYN-KRONES-UPDATE) measures the impact of cleaning burden on purchase choice, which is relevant to T1's premise that homebrewers seek professional-grade performance reducing waste. The test shows automated cleaning increases choice, supporting the idea that performance advantages drive willingness to pay a premium. New claim: Homebrewers will adopt Krones equipment primarily because they seek professional-grade performance that reduces waste and improves product consistency, leading to higher willingness to pay for premium equipment.. Evidence: SYN-KRONES-UPDATE.
The investigation stopped before a recommendation (repeated errors).

Who benefits: Consumers seeking to preserve food quality and save money; MULTIVAC benefits by capturing premium pricing and repeat purchases.. Predictions: Surveyed home cooks will indicate willingness to pay ≥€200 for a vacuum sealer.; Purchase intent will be higher when described as a professional-grade tool.; Repeat purchase rate for accessories will be ≥20% within 12 months..

T2: Health‑conscious consumers will adopt a consumer vacuum sealer if they perceive it as a way to preserve nutrients and reduce food waste, leading to purchase decisions based on environmental and health benefits. Who benefits: Consumers concerned about nutrition retention and waste reduction; MULTIVAC benefits by positioning the product as a sustainable, health‑focused offering and can command premium pricing.. Why behaviour changes: Growing awareness of food waste and nutrient loss drives demand for packaging that maintains freshness and quality; current evidence shows consumers already value vacuum sealing for freshness.. How value is captured: MULTIVAC can market the consumer model as a health‑preserving tool, price it at a premium (e.g., €200‑€300), and sell accessories and subscription services for reusable bags, capturing recurring revenue.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for products that reduce waste.; Marketing can effectively communicate nutrient retention benefits.; Distribution can reach health‑focused consumers (specialty retailers, online health platforms).. Predictions: Surveyed health‑conscious consumers will indicate willingness to pay ≥€200 for a vacuum sealer marketed on nutrient retention.; Purchase intent will be higher when highlighted as a waste‑reducing solution.; Repeat purchase rate for accessories will be ≥20% within 12 months when positioned as health‑focused..

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the application-kit offer and 72 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the template-software offer and 72 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. Test "Consumer Preference Test: Simplified vs Modular CNC" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase intent. Participants view two product concepts: (1) Simplified CNC router marketed as easy-to-use for home projects (2) Modular CNC router marketed as adaptable for multiple materials. Participants indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent on a 7-point scale. The test also collects demographic data (age, occupation, DIY experience).. Sample: 200 participants: 100 self-identified DIY woodworkers (recruited via woodworking forums and social media) and 100 small-batch manufacturers/hobbyists (recruited via makerspace networks and industry forums). Randomly assigned to view either the simplified or modular concept first.. Measure: Average WTP (EUR) and purchase intent score (1‑7) for each concept.. Predictions: T1: DIY woodworkers will show higher WTP and purchase intent for the simplified concept (WTP ≥ €1,200 and intent ≥ 5/7) compared to the modular concept.; T2: Small-batch manufacturers/hobbyists will show higher WTP and purchase intent for the modular concept (WTP ≥ €1,500 and intent ≥ 5/7) compared to the simplified concept.. Decision rule: If simplified WTP ≥ €1,200 and intent ≥ 5/7 among DIY woodworkers, proceed with a consumer-friendly proposition (supports T1). If modular WTP ≥ €1,500 and intent ≥ 5/7 among small-batch manufacturers/hobbyists, proceed with a modular proposition (supports T2). If neither meets thresholds, recommend no expansion. If both meet thresholds, prioritize the segment with the highest. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent for simplified vs modular concepts before committing resources. If the test meets the defined thresholds, proceed with a consumer-friendly proposition; otherwise, maintain the current B2B focus. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs. Compatible Home EV Heater" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with a controlled auction mechanism.. Sample: 300 German consumers who own or plan to purchase an electric vehicle (EV) within the next 12 months, recruited via an online panel.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and willingness to pay (WTP) for two product concepts: (1) Premium home EV heater (20% price premium over generic alternatives, marketed as automotive-grade, premium performance). (2) Specialized home EV heater (same price as generic alternatives, marketed as the only compatible solution for the EV brand’s charging network).. Predictions: T1: Purchase intent for the premium product will be at least 15% higher than for the specialized product, because consumers trust the automotive brand and are willing to pay a premium for performance and reliability.; T2: Purchase intent for the specialized product will be at least 15% higher than for the premium product, because consumers need compatibility with their specific EV charging setup and value reliability over brand trust.. Decision rule: If premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt premium proposition (supports T1). If specialized purchase intent ≥ 45% and premium purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt specialized proposition (supports T2). If neither meets threshold → no expansion recommended. If both meet threshold →. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium home EV heater versus a specialized compatible heater. If the test meets the 15% threshold for the premium proposition, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer line; otherwise, maintain B2B focus. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated result SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer purchase decisions, brand trust, or compatibility preferences for a home EV charging use case. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1. New claim: Consumers will adopt Eberspächer’s differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a premium, reliable solution for a specific use case (e.g., home EV charging comfort), because they trust the brand’s automotive heritage and are willing to pay a premium for performance and safety.. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium home EV heater versus a specialized compatible heater. If the test meets the 15% threshold for the premium proposition, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer line; otherwise, maintain B2B focus. Target customer: German EV owners planning to install home charging (estimated 300,000 per year, 10% of total EV owners).. Value proposition: A premium, automotive-grade home EV heater that offers superior performance and reliability, marketed as a trusted automotive brand extension.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the 10‑week, €18,000 Consumer Preference Test (X1) with 300 German EV owners to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium versus a specialized product.. Uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain because there is no direct evidence that consumers value brand trust or compatibility enough to pay a premium. The test will resolve this.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent for the premium product ≥ 45% and for the specialized product ≤ 35%, we would recommend pursuing the premium proposition (supporting T1).; If the test shows the opposite (e.g., specialized ≥ 45%, premium ≤ 35%), we would recommend pursuing the specialized proposition (supporting T2).; If neither meets the 15% threshold, we would recommend no expansion and maintain B2B focus.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

case.question: Should MULTIVAC Sepp Haggenmüller SE & Co. KG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing packaging machines and processing equipment for food, medical and industrial producers? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: Chamber sealers are used by professional chefs due to their ability to reliably achieve an airtight, mess-free seal — especially when it comes to liquids. The Anova Precision™ Chamber Vacuum Sealer brings that technology to your home at a fraction of the cost, with plenty of preset modes to do far more than just sealing.

FoodSaver® is the world’s #1 vacuum sealing system that helps avoid waste by keeping food fresher, longer. For over 30 years, FoodSaver has introduced innovative vacuum sealers, bags, and accessories to help people around the world avoid food waste, enjoy their food at its freshest, and save thousands of dollars each year.
This time, I decided to try something new. I had heard of the chamber sealers from hunting buddies but thought they were too pricey for my needs.
Baseline chamber machines are therefore the ideal vacuum packaging solution for butchers´shops, restaurants, hotels, chees dairies, direct marketing companies and farm shops.

Chamber vacuum sealers, while representing a smaller market share, are gaining popularity among serious home cooks and culinary enthusiasts who require professional-grade sealing capabilities for sous vide cooking and bulk food processing.

MULTIVAC tabletop chamber machines can be used very flexibly due to their compact dimensions. This means they are an ideal packaging solution for butchers, cheese dairies, restaurants, hotels, direct sellers and supermarkets as well as for a wide range of consumer goods.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify MULTIVAC investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B packaging and processing equipment, and identify what evidence would support that investment.. Constraints: Limited to publicly available information; financial and contractual details may not be public.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.; Need to verify current reach to individual buyers and identify specific consumer use cases.; Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to market for a consumer proposition.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home food packaging, small‑batch medical supplies) with a new product or service.; 2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding consumer‑friendly features or packaging solutions without creating a separate consumer brand.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B packaging machines and processing equipment for food, medical, pharmaceutical, and industrial producers..

Test "Consumer Purchase Intent Test for Professional vs Health Framing" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a MULTIVAC tabletop chamber vacuum sealer (specifications, price €250). They are randomly assigned to one of two framing conditions: (A) Professional-grade framing emphasizing sous vide cooking, bulk food processing, and professional-chef reliability; (B) Health‑focused framing emphasizing nutrient retention, waste reduction, and health benefits. Participants indicate: (1) likelihood to purchase on a 1‑10 scale; (2) maximum price they would pay; (3) likelihood to recommend to a friend. The test. Sample: 200 adult U.S. home cooks/culinary enthusiasts recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and cooking frequency.. Measure: Primary outcome: average purchase intent score (1‑10) for each framing condition. Secondary outcomes: average maximum price willing to pay and average recommendation likelihood.. Predictions: T1: Professional framing will yield higher purchase intent than health framing (difference ≥ 1.5 points on 10‑point scale).; T2: Health framing will yield higher purchase intent than professional framing (difference ≥ 1.5 points on 10‑point scale).. Decision rule: If professional framing ≥ 1.5 points higher than health framing, proceed with professional‑grade consumer proposition (supports T1). If health framing ≥ 1.5 points higher than professional framing, proceed with health‑focused proposition (supports T2). If neither framing meets the threshold, recommend no expansion. If both meet the threshold,. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home cooks and culinary enthusiasts who value professional-grade sealing capabilities for sous vide cooking and bulk food processing, priced at a premium (e.g., €250) and sold through specialty retailers and online channels. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home cooks and culinary enthusiasts who value professional-grade sealing capabilities for sous vide cooking and bulk food processing, priced at a premium (e.g., €250) and sold through specialty retailers and online channels. Target customer: Home cooks and serious amateur chefs who cook for family and friends, and who are willing to pay a premium for professional-grade kitchen tools.. Value proposition: A MULTIVAC tabletop chamber vacuum sealer that delivers professional-grade airtight sealing for sous vide cooking, bulk food processing, and mess-free sealing, enabling consumers to achieve restaurant-quality results at home.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Purchase Intent Test (200 participants, €18,000, 10 weeks) to measure purchase intent under professional vs health framing. Use the 1.5-point threshold to decide whether to proceed with professional-grade or health. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market, willingness to pay a premium, and the competitive landscape of existing vacuum sealers are uncertain. The test will resolve these uncertainties.. Would change if: If the test shows health framing yields at least 1.5 points higher purchase intent than professional framing, we would shift to a health‑focused proposition.; If neither framing meets the threshold, we would recommend no expansion.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: Bostik is pleased to announce that a curated selection of its professional-grade sealants and adhesives is now available for purchase on Amazon. This strategic move brings Bostik’s trusted solutions directly to consumers and contractors, providing convenient access to high-performance products for common household and jobsite applications

With a DIY and consumer range of more than 2,000 products, our brands are trusted for a wide range of applications. Our presence extends over 120 countries, allowing us to service retailers worldwide.
Sika offers a complete range of construction and landscaping products, including the renowned Sakrete products, perfectly suited to the needs of homeowners and contractors.

Explore Sika’s range of DIY sealants, designed to deliver professional results for home improvement and maintenance projects. Suitable for a variety of interior and exterior applications, these easy-to-use products offer excellent adhesion, flexibility and durability on common building surfaces.

Sika’s specialized solutions (e.g., roofing systems, industrial flooring, structural adhesives) often require trained applicators and strict adherence with technical standards. These products are not marketed for DIY or general retail because improper application could lead to performance failures or safety hazards.

In 2019, four in 10 home improvements were do-it-yourself projects. Yet, despite DIY spending levels remaining relatively stable since 2015, the share of DIY spending that year as it related to all of home improvement fell to a new low, 17% of total home improvement spending.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Sika AG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B construction chemicals, sealants, and adhesives, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.. Constraints: Limited public information on Sika’s current consumer reach and sales channels.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Evidence must come from public sources; internal company data may not be available.; Any recommendation must consider Sika’s existing B2B product portfolio and market presence.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual homeowners or DIY enthusiasts for a specific use case (e.g., home waterproofing, flooring installation).; 2) Expand into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., professional contractors purchasing for residential projects).; 3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on existing B2B construction chemicals, sealants, and adhesives.; 4) License Sika’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Sika’s own consumer brand..

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

The description emphasizes either premium positioning (safety, reliability, industrial reputation) or low-cost positioning (price discount, industrial scale). Participants indicate whether they would purchase the cable and the maximum price they would pay. The test is run with 500 private drivers (private EV owners, DIY enthusiasts) in Germany.. Sample: 500 German private drivers (private EV owners, DIY enthusiasts) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and region.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and maximum price willing to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: At least 30% of participants exposed to the premium description will indicate purchase intent, and their average maximum price will be at least 20% above competitor pricing.; T2: At least 40% of participants exposed to the low-cost description will indicate purchase intent, and their average maximum price will be at least 10% below competitor pricing.. Decision rule: If the premium group meets its threshold (purchase intent ≥ 30% and average price ≥ 20% premium) and the low-cost group does not meet its threshold (purchase intent ≥ 40% and average price ≥ 10% discount), conclude that the premium proposition aligns with T1. If both meet their thresholds, conclude that both strategies can work and further testing is needed. If neither meets its threshold, conclude that. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed consumer preference test (X1) to validate whether a premium-priced, safety/industrial-reputation-based proposition would achieve purchase intent and price tolerance among private drivers. If the test meets its thresholds, proceed to develop a limited consumer offering; otherwise, maintain focus on industrial B2B. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

How value is captured: Biesse captures value through premium pricing, higher-margin accessories, and long-term service contracts, leveraging its existing brand reputation in the professional market.. Assumptions: DIY users currently purchase CNC machines primarily through online marketplaces or specialty retailers.; Biesse can design a consumer-grade model without compromising core professional features.; Price sensitivity for this segment is within the €1,000–€5,000 range.. Test "Consumer vs Partner Branding Test" between T1; T2. Method: Create two identical online listings for a Biesse-branded CNC router: (1) a direct-to-consumer listing sold through Biesse’s own e-commerce platform at a €2,500 price point; (2) a co‑branded listing sold through a major retail partner (e.g., Amazon) at the same price, featuring Biesse’s professional logo and a brief description emphasizing the partnership. Both listings are promoted via social media and targeted ads to hobbyist CNC users.. Sample: Target 5,000 hobbyist CNC enthusiasts identified through social media groups, DIY forums, and online marketplaces. Recruit 2,000 for each listing (1,000 direct, 1,000 partner).. Measure: Conversion rate (percentage of visitors who place a deposit) and average order value for each listing.. Predictions: T1: The direct listing will convert at least 5% of visitors and have an average order value of €2,500, while the partner listing will convert <3% and have an average order value <€2,000.; T2: The partner listing will convert at least 5% of visitors and have an average order value of €2,500, while the direct listing will convert <3% and have an average order value <€2,000.. Decision rule: If the direct listing converts ≥5% and partner listing converts <3%, proceed with a consumer‑focused direct‑to‑retail proposition (supports T1). If partner listing converts ≥5% and direct listing converts <3%, proceed with a partner‑branded retail proposition (supports T2). If both listings convert <3%,. Cost: 18000 euros, 12 weeks.

Why behaviour changes: These manufacturers currently use manual tools or basic CNC machines; a Biesse consumer router would lower the barrier to entry for small-batch production, enabling them to increase output without significant investment in dedicated tooling. How value is captured: Biesse would capture value through volume sales of the consumer router, bundled software/support packages, and potential co‑branding opportunities with established small‑batch brands.. Participants view product description and pricing for a Biesse consumer CNC router. They indicate willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale and choose a preferred purchase channel (direct showroom, online marketplace, or retail store).. Sample: 500 DIY woodworkers (recruited via hobbyist forums) and 500 small‑batch manufacturers (recruited via makerspace networks and Etsy). Randomly split each group into two halves: half see a precision‑focused description, half see a speed‑of‑setup description.. Measure: Average WTP (EUR) for precision version vs speed version, and channel preference (showroom vs online vs retail). Secondary measure: self‑identified primary use case (personal projects vs small‑batch production).. Predictions: T1: DIY woodworkers will show higher WTP and higher showroom preference for the precision version, while small‑batch manufacturers will show higher WTP and higher online/retail preference for the speed version.; T2: Small‑batch manufacturers will show higher WTP and higher showroom/online preference for the speed version, while DIY woodworkers will show higher WTP and higher retail preference for the precision version.. Decision rule: If the average WTP difference between precision and speed versions exceeds €150 for the group that identifies as DIY woodworkers, proceed with a precision‑focused consumer proposition. If the difference exceeds €150 for the group that identifies as small‑batch. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Who benefits: Nabtesco, individual consumers, and the broader market for smart home technology.. Why behaviour changes: The increasing adoption of smart home technology and consumer service robots creates a market gap for a company like Nabtesco to offer tailored, integrated solutions that enhance user experience and convenience.. How value is captured: By developing and marketing a specialized robotic solution that seamlessly integrates with existing smart home ecosystems, Nabtesco can capture value through: 
- Premium pricing for advanced, integrated systems.
- Increased market share in . Assumptions: The global trend towards automation and AI in the home will continue.; Nabtesco has the technical expertise to develop and manufacture such robots.; There is a willingness among consumers to invest in smart home technology and robotic solutions.. Predictions: A 15% increase in sales of Nabtesco's robotic equipment within the next 3 years if the differentiated proposition is successfully launched.; A 20% growth in market share in the smart home robotics segment within 5 years..

Test "Consumer Demand Test" between T1; T2. Method: Survey and Interviews. Sample: 1000 individual consumers in target markets (e.g., US, Japan, Germany) split evenly between existing Nabtesco customers and potential new customers.. Measure: Willingness to purchase and perceived value of (1) a smart home-integrated service robot for a specific task (cleaning, pet care, elderly assistance) and (2) a premium automatic door system with AI integration.. Predictions: T1: Consumers in target markets express higher willingness to purchase and assign greater perceived value to a smart home-integrated service robot, leading to increased sales.; T2: Consumers in target markets express higher willingness to purchase and assign greater perceived value to a premium automatic door system with AI integration, outperforming the service robot.. Decision rule: If the difference in willingness to purchase and perceived value between the two products exceeds €50 (based on a €100 average price point), Nabtesco should prioritize development of the differentiated consumer proposition.. Cost: 5000 euros, 6 weeks.

case.question: Should Krones AG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing filling, packaging and process-technology lines for beverage and liquid-food producers? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

In light of the current transformation in the beverage and liquid-food industry as well as rising demands for sustainable, competitive and efficient products, Krones is restructuring its profitable and growing Compact Class line of business, which delivers machines and lines for the small and medium output range.

Designed for small to mid-sized craft breweries, the CRAFT-STAR® brewhouse line is available in two sizes, handling batches of either 20hl or 40hl of hot wort. Pre-assembled, wired and tested in Germany, CRAFT-STAR® is a compact system with integrated control cabinet and base frame that doubles up as a practical operator platform.
The home beer brewing machine market size was estimated at USD 213.4 million in 2025 and is expected to reach USD 237.9 million in 2026.

With the aid of our innovative, value-added solutions, our dense global service network and reliable completion of projects for our international customers, we are able to obtain adjusted prices despite the cost trend. Despite the ongoing intense competition for orders, we are sticking to our disciplined price strategy.
It is the ideal brewing device for switching from hobby to commercial brewing, for example as an introduction for caterers who want to offer their own beer to their guests.

Test "Subscription vs Premium Integrated Purchase Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice experiment with a sample of 200 small brewers and batch producers (recruited via industry forums and social media). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two scenarios: (A) Subscription model: monthly fee for a brewhouse with scheduled maintenance and service; (B) Premium integrated purchase: one-time purchase of a Krones integrated brewhouse with no upfront cost. Both scenarios describe the same brewhouse (CRAFT-STAR 20hl) with identical performance claims (downtime reduction, yield increase). Participants choose which. Sample: 200 small brewers and batch producers (100 per arm) recruited via industry forums and social media. Measure: Choice: Subscription (A) vs Premium Purchase (B). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale (1‑ €2,000‑ €4,000).. Predictions: T1: At least 60% of participants will choose the premium purchase (B) and indicate a WTP of at least €2,500, indicating they value reliability and are willing to pay for it.; T2: At least 60% of participants will choose the subscription (A) and indicate a WTP of at least €1,500, indicating they prefer lower upfront cost and cash‑flow flexibility.. Decision rule: If the proportion choosing premium purchase (B) ≥ 60% and WTP ≥ €2,500, proceed to develop a premium integrated consumer proposition. If the proportion choosing subscription (A) ≥ 60% and WTP ≥ €1,500, proceed to develop a subscription/leasing model. If neither condition is met, conclude that. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, conduct a low‑cost choice experiment (as proposed) to test whether small brewers prefer a premium integrated purchase or a subscription model. Use the results to decide whether to develop a premium integrated line or a subscription/leasing model. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated evidence SYN-KRONES-UPDATE concerns automated cleaning versus manual cleaning for a compact brewing system and does not address premium integrated purchase versus subscription models. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1. New claim: Home brewers and small batch producers will adopt Krones equipment if they perceive it as a premium, integrated solution that reduces downtime and improves yield, because they value reliability and consistency in their production.. Evidence: SYN-KRONES-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, conduct a low‑cost choice experiment (as proposed) to test whether small brewers prefer a premium integrated purchase or a subscription model. Use the results to decide whether to develop a premium integrated line or a subscription/leasing model. Target customer: Small brewers and batch producers (100‑200 hl) who require reliable, efficient machinery for consistent product quality.. Value proposition: A premium integrated brewhouse that reduces downtime, increases yield, and provides a single, high‑performance asset, sold directly by Krones with no upfront cost.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed choice experiment (200 participants, 10 weeks) to measure choice and willingness to pay for a premium integrated purchase versus a subscription model.. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Direct-to-Consumer vs. Aftermarket Price Sensitivity Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are recruited from Italy, Germany, and the United States (markets with strong motorcycle/off-road culture). They are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a premium direct-to-consumer (DTC) offer for a Brembo brake kit (e.g., €750 for a motorcycle kit). Group B sees the same kit priced at €250 (aftermarket price). Both groups are asked: "Would you purchase this kit at the offered price?" (yes/no).. Sample: 300 participants (100 per group). Participants are screened for self-identified motorcycle/off-road enthusiasts (e.g., have ridden for >5 years, own a motorcycle/off-road vehicle).. Measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of participants who select "yes" to the DTC offer).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show a purchase intent rate of at least 30% (indicating willingness to pay premium for a branded DTC kit).; T2: Group B will show a purchase intent rate of at least 30% (indicating willingness to pay aftermarket price for a branded DTC kit).. Decision rule: If Group A’s purchase intent rate ≥ 30% and Group B’s ≤ 20%, proceed to develop a differentiated DTC proposition targeting enthusiasts. If both rates ≤ 20%, no expansion. If Group A ≥ 30% and Group B ≥ 30%,. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 72 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Digital Refund Convenience Test" between T1; T2. Method: Run a 12‑week pilot in a mid‑size city (e.g., 200,000 residents) offering two versions of a digital refund app: (1) a basic version with 10% digital refund and drop‑off at a nearby collection point; (2) a premium version with 10% digital refund and drop‑off from home via a mobile app. Track weekly drop‑off numbers for each version. Also collect survey data on perceived convenience (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (binary).. Sample: 2,000 residents who have used a reverse vending machine in the past 12 months, recruited via local panels and social media.. Measure: Number of containers dropped off per week for each version; average convenience score; proportion of participants who would pay a premium for home drop‑off.. Predictions: T1: The basic version will achieve at least 500 drop‑offs per week and a convenience score above 7; the premium version will achieve at least 300 drop‑offs per week and a convenience score above 8.; T2: The premium version will achieve at least 500 drop‑offs per week and a convenience score above 7; the basic version will achieve fewer than 300 drop‑offs per week and a convenience score below 7.. Decision rule: If the premium version achieves at least 500 drop‑offs per week and a convenience score above 7, proceed to develop a full consumer proposition for home drop‑off. If the basic version achieves at least 500 drop‑offs per week and a convenience score above 7, proceed to develop a full consumer proposition for collection points. If neither version meets the threshold, conclude there is. Cost: 18000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed Digital Refund Convenience Test to empirically compare consumer adoption of a basic drop‑off at a collection point versus a premium drop‑off from home. The test will determine whether consumers prefer the convenience of home drop‑off and are willing to pay a premium, or if they still rely on existing collection points. The €18,000, 12‑week pilot can be executed within the budget and time constraints, Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated result SYN-TOMRA-UPDATE concerns a hypothetical test of doorstep versus store drop-off collection, not consumer adoption of a digital refund system. It does not address T1's claim about consumer convenience and willingness to pay for digital refunds, so it neither supports nor contradicts T1. New claim: Consumers will adopt a direct-to-consumer digital refund system for empty beverage containers because they seek convenience and want to be paid immediately, bypassing traditional reverse vending machine locations.. Evidence: SYN-TOMRA-UPDATE.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 32 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. Test "Consumer Preference Test: Direct‑to‑Consumer Offering vs Subscription Model" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants view a product description of a compact automated storage unit (specifications, benefits, price). They are then presented with two purchase options: (A) Direct‑purchase at full price (EUR 1,500), (B) Subscription‑based offering with monthly fee (EUR 50) and installation/maintenance included. They choose which option they would select and provide a brief explanation. The test is run with 200 participants (100 per arm) over 12 weeks.. Sample: 200 homeowners and small‑business owners recruited via online panels, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.. Measure: Purchase intent (percentage selecting option A or B) and primary reason cited for choice (e.g., "direct purchase cheaper," "subscription reduces upfront cost").. Predictions: T1: Direct‑purchase intent ≥ 40% and subscription intent ≤ 30% (favors T1).; T2: Subscription intent ≥ 40% and direct purchase intent ≤ 30% (favors T2).. Decision rule: If direct‑purchase intent ≥ 40% and subscription intent ≤ 30%, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home storage (supports T1). If subscription intent ≥ 40% and direct purchase intent ≤ 30%, develop a subscription‑based service (supports T2). If neither condition is met, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to validate demand and willingness to pay for a direct‑purchase model before committing resources. If the test shows direct‑purchase intent ≥ 40% and subscription intent ≤ 30%, proceed with a home‑storage offering; otherwise, maintain current B2B focus. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Test "Premium vs Compliance Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase intent. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: (A) Premium messaging emphasizing quality, reliability, and reduced production time; (B) Compliance messaging emphasizing regulatory-compliant, easy-to-use equipment. Both conditions describe a Krones homebrew machine at a premium price (e.g., €3,500). After viewing the assigned message, participants indicate purchase intent on a 0‑10 scale and willingness to pay a premium (e.g., 15‑20% above €3,500).. Sample: 200 homebrewers/small‑batch food producers recruited via hobbyist forums and industry lists, balanced for geographic region and experience.. Measure: Purchase intent score (0‑10) and willingness to pay premium (percentage above €3,500).. Predictions: T1: Condition A (Premium messaging) will achieve at least 15% higher purchase intent and willingness to pay premium than Condition B (Compliance messaging).; T2: Condition B (Compliance messaging) will achieve at least 15% higher purchase intent and willingness to pay premium than Condition A (Premium messaging).. Decision rule: If Condition A’s average purchase intent ≥ 7.5 and willingness to pay premium ≥ 15% above €3,500, proceed with premium‑focused consumer proposition. If neither condition meets both thresholds, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 letters of intent for the rental offer and 32 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Homeowner vs Small Business Digital Campaign Test" between T1; T2. Method: Run two parallel digital campaigns targeting distinct segments: homeowners and small businesses. Each campaign will offer a limited‑time, discounted price for a Kardex consumer‑branded vertical lift module (VLM). Track conversion rate (purchase intent) and willingness to pay (WTP) within the 12‑week test period.. Sample: 1) Homeowner campaign: 1,000 Swiss homeowners (aged 25‑55) recruited via online panels, targeted based on self‑reported home storage needs and interest in smart home solutions. 2) Small Business campaign: 1,000 small business owners (50‑250 employees) recruited via business directories and industry forums, targeted based on self‑reported inventory management challenges and interest in automated storage.. Measure: 1) Conversion rate: percentage of exposed users who click "Learn More" and complete a purchase intent form. 2) Average willingness to pay (WTP): maximum price willing to pay for a 2‑unit module (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Homeowner conversion rate ≥ 10% and average WTP ≥ EUR 2,500.; T2: Small Business conversion rate ≥ 8% and average WTP ≥ EUR 1,800.. Decision rule: If homeowner conversion ≥ 10% AND average WTP ≥ EUR 2,500, proceed with differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners. If small business conversion ≥ 8% AND average WTP ≥ EUR 1,800, proceed with differentiated consumer proposition targeting small businesses. If neither threshold met, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.
