sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the application-kit offer and 32 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Predictions: T1: Hobbyists exposed to premium messaging will show a higher average WTP and purchase intent than those exposed to professional messaging.; T2: Professionals exposed to professional messaging will show a higher average WTP and purchase intent than those exposed to premium messaging.. Test "Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs Subscription Pricing" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two product descriptions and pricing options. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners in Switzerland who report limited storage space and interest in home organization. They are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: (A) Premium home storage system (description emphasizing space‑saving, modern design, and price at 1.5x the baseline price of a comparable manual. Sample: 200 participants (100 per condition). Measure: Purchase intent measured on a 0‑10 scale ("Would you buy this product?") and willingness to pay (WTP) measured as the maximum price they would pay.. Predictions: T1: Condition A will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Condition B, because consumers value premium, space‑saving solutions and are willing to pay more for perceived value.; T2: Condition A will show lower purchase intent and WTP than Condition B, because consumers prefer subscription service that reduces upfront cost and provides convenience.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent in Condition A exceeds Condition B by at least 10 percentage points AND the average WTP in Condition A exceeds Condition B by at least 10% (e.g., Condition A WTP = 120% of baseline price, Condition B WTP = 90% of baseline price), then T1 is supported. If the. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home storage, emphasizing premium, space‑saving design and convenience, and test demand through a controlled survey experiment. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-KARDEX-UPDATE concerns a rental versus purchase choice for a compact automated storage module, not consumer demand for premium home storage. It does not address T1’s core premise that consumers value premium, space‑saving design and are willing to pay a premium price. Therefore T1 remains unchanged. New claim: Consumers will adopt Kardex’s automated storage solutions for home use if they perceive the system as a premium, space‑saving product that reduces clutter and increases productivity, and if price aligns with perceived value.. Evidence: SYN-KARDEX-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home storage, emphasizing premium, space‑saving design and convenience, and validate demand through a controlled survey experiment. Target customer: Homeowners in Switzerland and nearby markets who report limited storage space and interest in home organization, particularly tech‑savvy, urban residents.. Value proposition: A Kardex‑branded automated storage system that combines space‑saving design, proven performance, and a subscription‑based service model to reduce upfront cost and provide ongoing support.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (200 participants, 8 weeks, €15,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium‑priced home storage system versus a subscription‑based model.. Uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay a premium price for home storage; the size of the addressable market; competitive response from established consumer storage brands; and the feasibility of delivering a subscription‑based service at scale.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent for the premium offering is at least 10 percentage points higher than for the subscription offering, and willingness to pay is at least 10% higher, confidence in T1 would increase.; If the test shows strong preference for the subscription model (e.g., higher intent and willingness to pay for a lower‑priced offering), T2 would become more plausible.; If no significant difference is observed between the two offerings, the case for either theory would weaken.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the running-cost offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Participants are randomly assigned to one of two product descriptions: (A) Professional-grade vacuum sealer marketed for sous vide cooking and bulk food processing; (B) Health-focused vacuum sealer marketed for nutrient retention and waste reduction. Both descriptions include price point (€200). Participants indicate whether they would purchase and the maximum price they would pay. The. Sample: 500 German adults aged 25-55 who have purchased home kitchen appliances in the past year, recruited via an online panel.. Measure: Average willingness-to-pay (WTP) in euros for each product description, and binary purchase intent (yes/no).. Predictions: T1: Average WTP for professional-grade description will be at least €200 and significantly higher than for health-focused description.; T2: Average WTP for health-focused description will be at least €200 and significantly higher than for professional-grade description.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for professional-grade description exceeds the average WTP for health-focused description by at least €20, we conclude T1 is more likely. If the opposite difference is at least €20, we conclude T2 is more likely. If the difference is less than €20, we. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. Test "Home Storage Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions. Sample: 400 Swiss consumers aged 25-55, recruited via panel, balanced for gender and region. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and maximum WTP (EUR) for two product concepts: (1) Standalone home storage unit priced at 20% premium over standard storage (e.g., €1,200 vs €1,000). (2) Subscription-based home storage kit with hardware, installation, maintenance, and consumables, priced at €1,500 per year.. Predictions: T1: Purchase intent for the standalone unit will be at least 15% and WTP will exceed €1,000; subscription intent will be low (e.g., <5%).; T2: Purchase intent for the subscription kit will be at least 10% and WTP will exceed €1,500; standalone intent will be low (e.g., <5%).. Decision rule: If standalone purchase intent ≥15% and subscription purchase intent <10%, proceed with a direct-to-consumer standalone launch. If subscription purchase intent ≥10% and standalone intent <5%, proceed with a subscription-based model. If both meet thresholds, consider a hybrid. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed Home Storage Preference Test to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a standalone, premium-priced home storage unit. If the test meets the thresholds (purchase intent ≥15% and WTP >€1,000), proceed to develop a direct-to-consumer standalone offering; otherwise, consider a subscription model or no expansion. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Run the proposed Home Storage Preference Test to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a standalone, premium-priced home storage unit. If the test meets the thresholds (purchase intent ≥15% and WTP >€1,000), proceed to develop a direct-to-consumer standalone offering; otherwise, consider a subscription model or no expansion. Target customer: Swiss consumers aged 25-55 who need efficient home storage and are willing to pay a premium for automated solutions.. Value proposition: A differentiated, premium-priced automated home storage unit that solves real storage problems, leveraging Kardex’s intelligent retrieval technology to deliver faster access and reduced clutter.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the 10‑week, €15,000 online conjoint survey with 400 participants to collect purchase intent and willingness‑to‑pay data for the standalone unit and a subscription kit.. Uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay a premium for automated home storage; the size of the addressable market; competitive response from established consumer storage brands; and the feasibility of direct‑to‑consumer distribution.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Consumer Willingness-to-Pay Survey for a Consumer-Grade Biesse CNC Router" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are recruited from a panel of DIY woodworkers (defined as those who have built or modified wood projects in the past 12 months) and homeowners (defined as those who have undertaken home improvement projects requiring precision cutting). Each participant is shown a product description of a consumer-grade Biesse CNC router with specifications matching a desktop model (e.g., 12"x24" work. Sample: 200 participants: 100 DIY woodworkers and 100 homeowners. Recruitment via a panel provider to ensure geographic diversity.. Measure: Willingness-to-pay (WTP) in euros, measured as the maximum price participants would pay for the router. Secondary measures: purchase intent (binary) and perceived importance of precision and professional-grade features.. Predictions: T1: DIY woodworkers will report a WTP at least 1.5x the price of comparable consumer CNC routers (e.g., €2,500 vs €1,600).; T2: Homeowners will report a WTP at least 1.5x the price of comparable consumer CNC routers (e.g., €2,500 vs €1,600).. Decision rule: If the average WTP for DIY woodworkers exceeds €2,000 and the average WTP for homeowners exceeds €2,000, both theories are considered supported. If only one group exceeds €2,000, the theory for that group is supported, and the other is rejected. If neither group exceeds €2,000, both theories are rejected.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Conduct the proposed consumer willingness-to-pay survey (Test X1) to empirically test whether DIY woodworkers are willing to pay a premium for a consumer-grade Biesse CNC router. The survey will provide real demand evidence and help decide whether to invest in a differentiated consumer proposition or pursue other options. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Conduct the proposed consumer willingness-to-pay survey (Test X1) to empirically test whether DIY woodworkers are willing to pay a premium for a consumer-grade Biesse CNC router. The survey will provide real demand evidence and help decide whether to invest in a differentiated consumer proposition or pursue other options. Target customer: DIY woodworkers who have built or modified wood projects in the past 12 months and are willing to purchase directly from Biesse.. Value proposition: A consumer-grade Biesse CNC router that delivers professional-grade precision and digital control, sold directly to DIY woodworkers at a premium price, capturing margin on hardware and software while offering accessories and service. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the 10‑week, €15,000 willingness‑to‑pay survey with 200 participants (100 DIY woodworkers, 100 homeowners). Analyze results against the decision rule to determine whether to proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition or explore. Uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on DIY woodworker demand and willingness to pay a premium for a consumer‑grade router. The survey will resolve this uncertainty.. Would change if: If the survey shows average willingness‑to‑pay below €2,000 for DIY woodworkers, T1 would be rejected and the recommendation would shift to other expansion options or no expansion.; If the survey shows average willingness‑to‑pay above €2,000 for homeowners, T2 would be supported and the recommendation would shift to targeting homeowners instead of DIY woodworkers.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 32 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. Test "Consumer Preference Test: Hobby vs Sustainability Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants view a product description of a home spinning kit (specifying Rieter technology) and are randomly assigned to either a hobby-focused version (emphasizing creative fun and ease of use) or a sustainability-focused version (emphasizing recycled yarn and eco-credentials). They are then asked: "Would you purchase this kit at a price of €400?" (yes/no).. Sample: 300 crafters and hobbyists recruited via craft forums and social media, balanced for age and gender.. Measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and willingness to pay (binary).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when kit is marketed as a hobby (e.g., >40% say yes).; T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when kit is marketed as eco-friendly (e.g., >40% say yes).. Decision rule: If the proportion of participants who would purchase the kit under hobby messaging exceeds the proportion under sustainability messaging by at least 10 percentage points, proceed to develop a hobby-focused consumer proposition. If the opposite is true, proceed to develop a sustainability-focused. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 72 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Homebrewers and small‑batch food producers will purchase Krones equipment directly if they perceive it as a premium, sustainable, and time‑saving solution that reduces production costs and increases quality. Who benefits: Individual hobbyist brewers and small‑batch food producers who need reliable, efficient equipment for under‑10,000 L per batch.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers value reliability, ease of use, and environmental sustainability; they are willing to pay a premium for equipment that simplifies their production process and reduces waste.. How value is captured: Krones can capture value by pricing its consumer‑grade machines at a premium (e.g., €15,000‑€30,000 per unit) and offering subscription services for maintenance, capturing recurring revenue.. Assumptions: Homebrewers and small‑batch food producers are willing to invest in equipment that improves product quality and reduces labor.; Krones can design a consumer‑friendly product line that is easy to install and operate.; There is sufficient market awareness of Krones among this segment to drive direct purchases.. Predictions: If offered a direct‑to‑consumer product priced at €20,000 with a 2‑year warranty, at least 10% of surveyed homebrewers would express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.; Surveyed small‑batch food producers would report a willingness to pay a 20% premium for Krones equipment compared to competitors..

T2: Krones can capture value by offering a subscription‑based service for maintenance and consumables, enabling recurring revenue and a lower upfront purchase barrier for consumers. Who benefits: Homebrewers and small‑batch food producers who need reliable equipment but prefer lower initial cost and guaranteed support.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers value predictability and convenience; a subscription model removes the risk of equipment failure and simplifies cash flow, making them more willing to adopt Krones equipment.. How value is captured: Krones captures value through monthly or annual subscription fees (e.g., €150‑€250 per unit) and bundled consumables, generating recurring revenue and a higher lifetime value per customer.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a subscription fee for maintenance and consumables that covers normal wear and tear.; Krones can scale a subscription platform and delivery of consumables without significant additional overhead.; There is sufficient market awareness of Krones among this segment to drive subscription sign‑ups.. Predictions: If offered a subscription model with a 2‑year maintenance contract and consumables, at least 15% of surveyed homebrewers would subscribe within 12 weeks.; Small‑batch food producers would report a willingness to pay a 10% premium for a subscription‑based service compared to a one‑time purchase..

Test "Subscription vs Premium Direct Purchase Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice experiment with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 2,000 U.S. homebrewers and small‑batch food producers recruited via hobbyist forums, social media, and industry newsletters.. Measure: Proportion choosing the subscription model (WTP €150‑€250 per year) vs the premium direct‑purchase model (WTP €20,000‑€30,000). Secondary measure: stated maximum price for Krones equipment.. Predictions: T1: At least 35% will choose the premium direct purchase model, with a WTP of €25,000 or higher, indicating willingness to pay a premium for Krones equipment.; T2: At least 35% will choose the subscription model, with a WTP of €150‑€250 per year, indicating willingness to pay for a lower upfront cost and maintenance service.. Decision rule: If the proportion choosing the premium direct purchase model ≥ 35% and average WTP ≥ €25,000, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting premium direct buyers. If the proportion choosing the subscription model ≥ 35% and average WTP ≥ €150‑€250, proceed with a subscription‑based service. If neither condition is met, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting premium, direct‑purchase homebrewers and small‑batch food producers who value reliability, efficiency, and sustainability. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 72 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

In light of the current transformation in the beverage and liquid-food industry as well as rising demands for sustainable, competitive and efficient products, Krones is restructuring its profitable and growing Compact Class line of business, which delivers machines and lines for the small and medium output range.

It’s not only millions of beverage bottles and cans that are handled on Krones lines every day, the company’s solutions are also used in the food and stimulants industries, plus the chemical, cosmetics and pharmaceutical sectors.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Hobbyist Price Sensitivity Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are recruited from hobbyist CNC forums (e.g., Tormach, CNCZone) and offered a Gühring drill bit at a price 10‑20% below its usual retail price (e.g., €150 instead of €180). They are asked to indicate whether they would purchase it and, if so, the maximum price they would pay. The test runs for 4 weeks, with 200 participants expected to complete the survey.. Sample: 200 hobbyists who have posted about CNC projects in the past 12 months, recruited via forum announcements and social media.. Measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price willing to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: self‑reported importance of compatibility with existing CNC machines (1‑5 scale).. Predictions: T1: At least 30% of participants will indicate purchase intent at the discounted price, and compatibility will be ranked as the top purchase driver for at least 60% of those who would buy.; T2: At least 30% of participants will indicate purchase intent at the discounted price, and brand prestige will be ranked as the top purchase driver for at least 40% of those who would buy.. Decision rule: If purchase intent ≥ 30% AND compatibility ranks ≥ 60% of purchase‑intent group, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing compatibility. If purchase intent ≥ 30% AND prestige ranks ≥ 40% of purchase‑intent group, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing premium branding. If neither condition is met, conclude that. Cost: 15000 euros, 4 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 72 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 32 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. case.question: Should Kardex Holding AG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing automated storage and retrieval systems (vertical lift modules, carousels and AutoStore-based systems) for warehouses, factories and organisations? sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. T1: Consumers will adopt automated home storage if they perceive it as a premium, time‑saving solution, and are willing to pay a price premium for integrated, easy‑to‑use systems that reduce clutter and simplify inventory management. Who benefits: Consumers seeking efficient home storage and willingness to pay for convenience; Kardex would capture value through higher‑margin consumer sales and subscription services.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers shift from traditional storage solutions to automated systems when they experience the time and space savings, and when price sensitivity is offset by perceived long‑term convenience and reduced physical effort.. How value is captured: Kardex would sell consumer‑branded modules or kits through retail or direct channels, charge monthly or annual fees for software/service, and potentially offer subscription bundles that include consumables.. Assumptions: Consumers assess total cost of ownership (TCO) including installation, maintenance, and consumables.; Competition from low‑cost DIY storage solutions is limited.; Kardex can design a user‑friendly, aesthetically acceptable consumer product.; Distribution channels (retail, online) can be secured without major new investments.. Predictions: A survey of 500 households would show >30% indicating intent to purchase an automated home storage system priced at 1.5x the cost of a comparable manual unit.; Purchase intent would correlate with self‑reported time savings and reduced clutter worries.; Actual purchase rate would be lower than intent due to price sensitivity, resulting in a conversion rate of ~15%..

Who benefits: Consumers gain convenient storage without upfront purchase; retailers gain incremental sales and subscription revenue; Kardex gains volume sales and recurring revenue through bundled offerings.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers adopt automated storage when it is presented as a low‑risk, bundled service that aligns with existing home‑improvement workflows, eliminating the need for large upfront cash outlay and reducing perceived complexity.. Assumptions: Retailers or subscription platforms have existing customer databases and distribution channels.; Consumers trust bundled offerings from trusted home‑improvement brands.; Kardex can design a modular, easy‑to‑install system that fits standard home‑improvement packaging.; Subscription model provides predictable recurring revenue.. Predictions: A survey of 500 households would show >25% indicating intent to purchase a bundled automated storage kit if offered through a home‑improvement retailer.; Purchase intent would be higher among households that have previously purchased home‑improvement products from the same retailer.; Actual purchase rate would be driven by subscription uptake, with a conversion rate of ~10% for bundled offers..

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 72 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the template-software offer and 32 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. Predictions: T1: Purchase intent for the premium product will be at least 15% higher than for the specialized product, because consumers trust the automotive brand and are willing to pay a premium for performance and reliability.; T2: Purchase intent for the specialized product will be at least 15% higher than for the premium product, because consumers need compatibility with their specific EV charging setup and value reliability over brand trust.. Decision rule: If premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt premium proposition (supports T1). If specialized purchase intent ≥ 45% and premium purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt specialized proposition (supports T2). If neither meets threshold → no expansion recommended. If both meet threshold →. Constraints: Limited to public sources; internal company data may not be available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Need to verify current reach to individual buyers and identify specific consumer use cases.; Investment must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to market.. T1: Consumers will adopt Lapp components for home automation and electric vehicle charging if the company offers a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes ease of installation, reliability, and brand reputation from industrial leadership. Who benefits: Private electric car owners and DIY homeowners seeking reliable charging solutions and integrated automation.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers currently face high installation costs and compatibility issues with competing components. A differentiated offering that leverages Lapp’s industrial reputation for quality and reliability would reduce perceived risk and lower the. How value is captured: Lapp would capture value through premium pricing for consumer-grade components, direct-to-consumer sales channels, and potential licensing of its automation technology to consumer brands.. Assumptions: Consumers trust Lapp’s industrial reputation and are willing to pay a premium for proven reliability.; Installation costs for Lapp components are lower than competitors due to modular design and global logistics.; Lapp can reach individual buyers through existing sales network and online channels.. Predictions: In a test offering a consumer-branded EV charger with Lapp components, purchase intent among target consumers will be at least 15% higher than a generic competitor product.; Willingness to pay a 20% premium over generic alternatives will be observed in a price sensitivity survey.; Repeat purchase rate for Lapp’s consumer line will exceed 30% within 12 months..

T2: Consumers will adopt Lapp components for home automation and electric vehicle charging if the company offers a differentiated consumer proposition that leverages its automation expertise and provides integrated, easy-to-use control solutions, because consumers seek smart, connected devices that simplify daily routines. Who benefits: Private electric car owners and DIY homeowners who value smart home integration and want a seamless charging experience.. Why behaviour changes: Current consumer offerings often lack centralized control and require separate apps or hardware. A differentiated offering that combines Lapp’s automation technology with consumer-friendly interfaces would reduce the complexity of managing. How value is captured: Lapp would capture value through premium pricing for integrated control modules, subscription fees for cloud services, and partnerships with consumer brands to embed Lapp’s automation technology in smart home products.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for devices that simplify daily routines and reduce app clutter.; Lapp’s automation expertise can be adapted to consumer needs without major redesign.; There is sufficient consumer demand to justify dedicated development and marketing.. Predictions: In a test offering a consumer-branded smart charger with integrated automation controls, purchase intent will be at least 10% higher than a generic competitor product.; Willingness to pay a 15% premium for integrated controls will be observed in a price sensitivity survey.; Repeat purchase rate for Lapp’s consumer line will exceed 25% within 12 months..

Test "Consumer Proposition Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with randomized exposure to either a consumer-branded EV charger emphasizing ease of installation and industrial reputation (T1) or a consumer-branded smart charger emphasizing integrated automation controls (T2). Participants indicate purchase intent and willingness to pay.. Sample: 500 private electric car owners and DIY homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and region.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.. Predictions: T1: Purchase intent for the ease-of-installation proposition will be at least 15% higher than the generic competitor product.; T2: Purchase intent for the integrated automation proposition will be at least 10% higher than the generic competitor product.. Decision rule: If the observed difference in purchase intent between the test proposition and a generic competitor is >=15% (T1) or >=10% (T2), the respective theory is considered supported. If the difference is <10%, both theories remain uncertain.. Cost: 12000 euros, 10 weeks.

If the test meets the 15% purchase intent difference threshold, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for home automation and EV charging; otherwise, maintain the current B2B focus. The test is Target customer: Private electric car owners and DIY homeowners who need reliable, easy-to-install charging solutions and value industrial-grade quality.. Value proposition: A consumer-branded EV charger that leverages Lapp’s industrial reputation for reliability, ease of installation, and global logistics, offering a premium-priced, integrated solution that reduces installation complexity and perceived risk.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the Consumer Proposition Preference Test (X1) within the 12‑week timeframe and €12,000 budget, reporting results here.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent for the ease-of-installation proposition is at least 15% higher than a generic competitor, indicating T1 is supported and justifies investment.; If the test shows purchase intent for the integrated automation proposition is at least 10% higher, indicating T2 is supported and also justifies investment.; If the test fails to show a meaningful difference between the two propositions, both theories remain uncertain and further testing would be required.. T1: Developing a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, such as smart home integration or circular economy-focused solutions, could significantly increase Biesse's market share and revenue. This is because it addresses emerging trends among individual buyers in the wood, glass, stone, and advanced materials industries, who are increasingly seeking technology-driven, sustainable, and connected tools. Who benefits: Biesse S.p.A.. Why behaviour changes: Emerging trends in individual buyer behavior include a growing demand for smart home integration, circular economy solutions, and sustainable, connected products. These trends present opportunities to differentiate Biesse's existing product. How value is captured: By offering products that meet these emerging demands, Biesse can command premium pricing, attract new customers, and strengthen customer loyalty. Additionally, it can expand its market reach into new segments, such as smart home technology. Assumptions: Biesse's current product lines do not significantly incorporate smart home or circular economy features.; There is a market demand for smart home integrated and circular economy-focused wood processing machines.; Biesse has the technical expertise and manufacturing capabilities to develop such products.. Predictions: A 10% increase in market share within the wood processing segment within 2 years of launching a differentiated product.; A 15% increase in average order value for wood processing machines.; A 20% increase in customer loyalty among new and existing customers who purchase the differentiated product..

T2: Introducing a subscription-based model for software updates and remote support could also drive revenue and customer loyalty. This strategy leverages the increasing demand for digital services and remote access to machinery, especially in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. By offering continuous software improvements and technical assistance, Biesse can position itself as a technology partner rather than just a machi Who benefits: Biesse S.p.A.. Why behaviour changes: The pandemic accelerated the adoption of digital services and remote work, trends that are expected to persist. Customers, particularly in industrial manufacturing, are looking for more flexible and cost-effective maintenance solutions.. How value is captured: A subscription model allows Biesse to generate recurring revenue from existing customers. It also opens up opportunities for upselling additional services like premium support, training, and customized software solutions.. Assumptions: Biesse's products are increasingly software-driven and connected.; There is a market for digital services and remote support in industrial manufacturing.; Biesse has the technical infrastructure to support a subscription-based model.. Predictions: A 12% increase in recurring revenue within 3 years from subscription model introduction.; A 10% reduction in average downtime due to proactive software updates and remote support.; A 15% increase in customer retention rates for subscription customers..

Test "Biesse Market Share Test" between T1; T2. Method: Survey and Interview. Sample: 100 individual buyers in the wood, glass, stone, and advanced materials industries (50 per theory). Measure: Intent to purchase differentiated products (scale 1-5), current product satisfaction (scale 1-5), and perceived value of smart home/circular economy features (scale 1-5). Predictions: T1: Individuals in the wood, glass, stone, and advanced materials industries will show higher intent to purchase and satisfaction with, and higher perceived value of, products with smart home or circular economy features.; T2: Individuals will show higher intent to purchase and satisfaction with, and higher perceived value of, products with subscription-based software updates and remote support.. Decision rule: If the average intent to purchase score for T1 is 4.5 or higher, and for T2 is 4 or higher, then the respective theory is supported. This threshold accounts for some uncertainty and variability in responses.. Cost: 10000 euros, 6 weeks.
The investigation stopped before a recommendation (repeated errors).

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Who benefits: Individual hobbyists and small metalworking shops gain better results and longer tool life.. Why behaviour changes: If hobbyists believe Gühring tools deliver consistent, precise results and outlast competitors, they will choose them even at higher prices.. How value is captured: Gühring can charge premium prices for its brand reputation and quality, and capture value through direct-to-consumer sales or partnerships with specialty retailers.. Assumptions: Hobbyists and small workshops value precision and durability over cost.; They are willing to pay a premium for tools that meet their exacting standards.; They have access to information about Gühring’s reputation and performance.. Predictions: In a test offering a Gühring drill at a 20% premium price to a sample of 100 hobbyists, at least 60% will express intent to purchase.; Surveyed users will report higher satisfaction with hole accuracy and tool longevity compared to competitors..

T2: Hobbyists and small workshops will adopt Gühring’s precision tools if they can obtain them through convenient online channels and existing B2B relationships, reducing the need for a separate consumer brand. Why behaviour changes: If Gühring’s tools are already available via its B2B online shop and procurement systems, hobbyists will purchase them without seeking a new brand, leveraging existing relationships.. How value is captured: Gühring can increase sales volume by opening its B2B channels to individual buyers, capturing value through higher transaction frequency and reduced marketing costs.. Assumptions: Hobbyists are already aware of Gühring through industrial channels.; They trust the B2B online shop for purchasing industrial tools.; They are willing to pay a premium for tools they already know work well.. Predictions: In a test offering Gühring drills directly through the B2B shop to 100 hobbyists, at least 40% will place an order within 4 weeks.; Purchase intent will be higher than for a new consumer brand, indicating existing channel sufficiency..

Test "Hobbyist Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Recruit 200 hobbyists (100 per arm) via metalworking forums and social media. Randomly assign each participant to one of two conditions: Condition A: offer a Gühring drill at a 20% premium price (e.g., €120 instead of €100) with a brief description of precision and durability benefits. Condition B: offer the same drill at the same €100 price with no premium positioning, using the existing B2B online shop’s. Sample: 200 hobbyists (100 per arm). Measure: Purchase intent: binary “Would you buy this drill?” and willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7‑point scale.. Predictions: T1: Condition A will show at least 60% purchase intent and a WTP of at least €110, indicating hobbyists value premium positioning.; T2: Condition B will show at least 60% purchase intent and a WTP of at least €100, indicating they already purchase through B2B channels and price is secondary.. Decision rule: If purchase intent in Condition A ≥ 60% and WTP ≥ €110, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition (supports T1). If purchase intent in Condition B ≥ 60% and WTP ≥ €100, proceed with expanding B2B channels (supports T2). If neither condition meets thresholds, no expansion is. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed Hobbyist Purchase Intent Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a 20% premium-priced Gühring drill. If the test meets the thresholds (purchase intent ≥ 60% and WTP ≥ €110), proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition; otherwise, focus on expanding B2B channels or maintaining the current B2B-only model. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Run the proposed Hobbyist Purchase Intent Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a 20% premium-priced Gühring drill. If the test meets the thresholds (purchase intent ≥ 60% and WTP ≥ €110), proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition; otherwise, focus on expanding B2B channels or maintaining the current B2B-only model. Target customer: Individual hobbyists and small workshops (1‑10 employees) who need precision metalworking tools for personal or small‑scale projects.. Value proposition: A premium‑priced Gühring drill that delivers superior accuracy, durability, and brand reputation, sold directly to consumers via an online channel, leveraging existing B2B shop integration.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the Hobbyist Purchase Intent Test (X1) within the 12‑week budget, targeting 200 hobbyists (100 per arm) via metalworking forums and social media.. Uncertainty: The size of the hobbyist market for Gühring tools, willingness to pay a premium, and whether hobbyists already obtain tools through B2B channels are unknown. The test will resolve these uncertainties.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent below 60% or WTP below €110, the favoured theory would shift to T2 and the recommendation would be to expand B2B channels.; If additional evidence shows hobbyists already purchase Gühring tools through B2B channels at high volumes, T2 would become more likely and the recommendation would shift accordingly.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the running-cost offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Consumer Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Professional-Grade vs Health-Focused Vacuum Sealer" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two product descriptions: (A) Professional-grade vacuum sealer marketed for sous vide cooking and bulk food processing; (B) Health-focused vacuum sealer marketed for nutrient retention and waste reduction. Both descriptions include price point (€200). Participants indicate whether they would purchase and the maximum price they would pay. The. Sample: 500 German adults aged 25-55 who have purchased home kitchen appliances in the past year, recruited via an online panel.. Measure: Average willingness-to-pay (WTP) in euros for each product description, and binary purchase intent (yes/no).. Predictions: T1: Average WTP for professional-grade description will be at least €200 and significantly higher than for health-focused description.; T2: Average WTP for health-focused description will be at least €200 and significantly higher than for professional-grade description.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for professional-grade description exceeds the average WTP for health-focused description by at least €20, we conclude T1 is more likely. If the opposite difference is at least €20, we conclude T2 is more likely. If the difference is less than €20, we. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the application-kit offer and 32 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Who benefits: Individual consumers who receive digital refunds and can return containers from home, and retailers who gain foot traffic and can brand themselves as eco‑friendly.. Why behaviour changes: Convenience (no need to visit a redemption center) and digital refund (instant payout without cash) lower perceived effort and reduce barriers to participation.. How value is captured: TOMRA can charge a subscription fee for the app and service, or earn revenue from data on consumer return habits that can be sold to retailers or recycling programs.. T2: Consumers will adopt a consumer‑facing reverse vending machine (RVM) for residential deposit return if they receive a tangible cash refund (e.g., a voucher or coin return) that is easily redeemable at nearby retailers, because physical money provides immediate gratification and reduces trust concerns about digital refunds. Who benefits: Individual consumers who receive cash refunds and can redeem them for goods or services, and retailers who gain additional foot traffic and can partner to facilitate redemption.. Why behaviour changes: Physical cash eliminates the need for a digital refund mechanism and associated trust in app accuracy, making the return process more tangible and convenient for consumers.. How value is captured: TOMRA can charge a subscription fee for the cash‑return service, or earn revenue from retailer partnerships that share redemption revenue.. Assumptions: Consumers prefer physical cash refunds over digital refunds for deposit returns.; Retailers are willing to accept and redeem consumer‑generated RVM returns as a marketing incentive.; Regulatory frameworks permit cash refunds for consumer‑generated deposits.. Predictions: In a test offering cash refunds via a vending machine, at least 25% of participating households will redeem at least one refund within two weeks.; Surveyed satisfaction with cash refund will be rated “very satisfied” by at least 60% of users.; Retailers will report a measurable increase in purchases from customers who use the cash‑return service..

Owing to extraordinary restructuring expenses and transaction costs in connection with the acquisition of Barmag in the amount of CHF 54.2 million, Rieter closed the 2025 financial year with a net loss of CHF 63.4 million (2024: net profit of CHF 10.4 million).

Test "Market Viability Test: Differentiated Consumer Proposition" between T1; T2; T3. Method: Mixed Methods: Survey and Case Studies. Sample: 100 individual buyers: 50 current industrial spinning mill customers, 50 potential textile manufacturers focusing on sustainability (new market segment). Measure: 1.  Willingness to pay a premium for: (a) specialized spinning solutions (b) sustainable spinning solutions 2.  Current use of sustainable fibers 3. Interest in switching to Rieter's offerings. Predictions: T1: Increased willingness to pay for specialized solutions among new customers (sustainable fibers as a specific use case); T2: High willingness to pay for sustainable solutions across all respondents; T3: Moderate willingness to pay, with some current sustainable users and others hesitant to switch. T1: Consumers will adopt Lapp components for home automation if the company offers a differentiated, easy-to-install consumer product, leveraging its existing global sales network. Who benefits: Private homeowners seeking convenient, reliable charging solutions for electric vehicles and home appliances.. Why behaviour changes: Current consumer charging solutions are often complex and expensive, creating a barrier. A differentiated, consumer-friendly product that leverages Lapp’s existing global distribution would lower perceived risk and cost, making adoption. How value is captured: Lapp would capture value through premium consumer pricing, direct-to-consumer sales, and brand extension into the consumer market, leveraging its existing B2B sales channels.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a simple, reliable charging solution.; Lapp’s global sales network can reach individual buyers effectively.; The company can adapt existing components to meet consumer safety and aesthetic standards.. Who benefits: Private homeowners seeking hassle‑free, reliable charging solutions for electric vehicles and home appliances.. Why behaviour changes: Current consumer charging solutions often require professional installation and ongoing maintenance, creating high upfront cost and ongoing expense. A subscription model that includes installation, maintenance, and remote monitoring would. Test "Consumer Preference Test: Direct-to-Consumer vs Subscription Model" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with randomized exposure to either a direct-to-consumer (DTC) charging kit or a subscription-based charging kit, followed by willingness-to-pay (WTP) and purchase intent questions.. Sample: 500 private homeowners in Germany, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and region.. Measure: 1) Binary purchase intent (yes/no) for the presented kit. 2) Maximum WTP (EUR) for the kit. 3) Subscription retention rate (for the subscription model).. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the application-kit offer and 32 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the template-software offer and 72 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

case.question: Should Brembo N.V. develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing brake systems for vehicle manufacturers and replacement parts for the aftermarket? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for High‑Performance Brake Kits" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: (A) heritage/adjustability messaging emphasizing 50‑year motorsport heritage, market‑leading adjustability, and Italian design; (B) safety/durability messaging emphasizing proven off‑road performance, extreme‑condition reliability, and racing pedigree. Both groups see the same product description (Brembo GR‑PRO mountain‑bike brake kit) and are asked: "How much would you pay for this kit?" (. Sample: 300 individual mountain‑bikers and off‑road enthusiasts recruited via cycling forums and social media, balanced across age, gender, and riding experience.. Measure: Average willingness‑to‑pay (EUR) for the kit in each group.. Predictions: T1: Group A will report a higher average willingness‑to‑pay than Group B because heritage and adjustability justify premium pricing.; T2: Group B will report a higher average willingness‑to‑pay than Group A because safety and durability in extreme conditions justify premium pricing.. Decision rule: If Group A’s average willingness‑to‑pay exceeds Group B’s by at least €150 (a 10% premium over the €750 price point), we conclude T1 is more likely. If Group B’s average exceeds Group A’s by at least €150, we conclude T2 is more likely. If the difference is less than €150, we conclude both theories are uncertain and further evidence is needed.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (Test X1) to empirically compare heritage/adjustability messaging against safety/durability messaging. The test will determine whether consumers are willing to pay a premium for heritage-driven kits, which would support T1, or whether safety/durability messaging drives higher willingness to pay, which would support T2. The €15,000 budget and 12‑week timeline are sufficient‑ Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Who benefits: Gühring benefits by capturing sales from a growing segment of individual buyers who value precision and compatibility, expanding its consumer market beyond B2B.. Why behaviour changes: If hobbyists view Gühring as a trusted, compatible alternative that performs as well as higher‑priced competitors, they will purchase it instead of cheaper alternatives or continue using existing tools.. How value is captured: Gühring can price its tools competitively while maintaining its premium reputation, generating revenue from a new consumer segment without diluting its industrial brand.. Assumptions: Hobbyists and small workshops have sufficient budget for precision tools.; They prioritize reliability and compatibility over cost.; They are aware of Gühring through existing B2B channels or word of mouth.. Why behaviour changes: If hobbyists perceive Gühring as a brand that signifies high‑quality craftsmanship and expert‑level performance, they will choose it over cheaper alternatives even if the functional performance is similar.. How value is captured: Gühring can price its consumer line at a premium (e.g., 20‑30% above mainstream CNC tool brands) while leveraging its existing reputation for precision in industrial markets, capturing higher margins and brand equity.. Assumptions: Hobbyists value status and brand reputation in tools.; They are willing to pay more for a brand that signals expertise.; They are aware of Gühring through its industrial presence or word of mouth..
